title: Methods for Automated Equivalence Checking of Quantum Error-Correction Codes
authors: Maxie Bichmann, Ludwig Schmid, Robert Wille
abstract: Quantum error-correction code and circuit construction is an active field of research, motivating automated methods for identifying equivalent designs. We develop and evaluate automated strategies for deciding whether two descriptions of quantum error-correction codes are equivalent under specified transformations. We formalize permutation equivalence for stabilizer and CSS codes and local-Clifford equivalence for stabilizer codes within a unified framework that separates physical from representation freedom. We develop three decision strategies (group-action search, isomorphism-based methods, and constraint solving), together with invariants and signatures for preprocessing. The empirical evaluation shows that no paradigm dominates across equivalence notions, code families, and parameter ranges. We therefore combine their complementary strengths in input-dependent hybrid checkers following a staged Refute-Refine-Decide architecture. Mean hybrid runtimes remain below 10 s for most evaluated structured-code cases with $n \leq 37$; for inequivalent code instances with $n=144$, they are about 310 s for permutation and 16 s for local-Clifford equivalence.
summary: This work develops automated tools to check the equivalence of quantum error-correcting codes under transformations like qubit permutation or local Clifford operations. By combining group-action search, isomorphism techniques, and constraint solving, the authors create a robust, hybrid checker. This advances the field by providing practical, scalable methods to manage the inherent representation freedom in quantum code descriptions.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of automatically determining if two mathematical descriptions of Quantum Error-Correction (QEC) codes are equivalent under various physical and representation transformations.
main_result: The authors developed hybrid checkers combining group-action search, isomorphism methods, and constraint solving, achieving practical runtimes for structured codes while demonstrating that no single algorithmic paradigm is universally superior.
method: They formalize equivalence notions (permutation and local-Clifford) within a unified framework and combine three distinct algorithmic strategies into a staged Refute-Refine-Decide architecture.
model_or_system: The focus is on Quantum Error-Correction Codes (QECCs), specifically stabilizer and CSS codes, which are analyzed using their binary symplectic representations (symplectic tableaux). The ambiguity arises from both physical transformations (like qubit relabeling) and representation choices.
key_observables: Mean runtimes for equivalence checking, the fraction of distinguished qubit pairs ($ ar{q}$), and the number of SAT solver decisions required for refutation.
important_parameters: Code length ($n$), stabilizer rank ($r$), and the specific equivalence notion (permutation vs. local-Clifford).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the ability to map codes to algebraic structures (symplectic tableaux) and assumes the applicability of linear algebra techniques for constraint solving.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the ambiguity requiring checking (e.g., Steane code realizations), the separation of physical vs. representation freedom, and runtime comparisons between different encoding methods (Full-Group vs. Matroid-Circuit).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by defining the degrees of freedom (physical vs. representation), develops and compares three distinct algorithmic strategies (group-action, isomorphism, constraint solving), and concludes by proposing a hybrid, staged checker architecture with empirical performance evaluation.
why_interesting: While focused on abstract coding theory, the need to automate the comparison of complex, high-dimensional structures (like code generators) using hybrid computational methods is relevant to characterizing quantum states or Hamiltonians derived from physical models.
